6.t: PRINCIPAL'S
MESSAGE
THE year 1979 reminds us that Wah Yan College is now 60 years old，
having been opened on December 10th，， 1919. Our founder, Mr. Peter
Tsui Yan Sau is, happily, still with us, having celebrated his ninetieth birthday
some years ago. The oldest of our past students are beginning to retire from
active life and some of*them have grandsons now in the school. It is such
ties as these that help so much to build up the sense of family life in the
school, communicating itself to all who join Wah Yan and make them feel，
on leaving, that they are leaving home.
The past year is. worthy of being the Diamond Jubilee Year. The breadth
and quality of educational activities have culminated in some outstanding
performances in widely different fields. The Certificate Examination results
of the year 1978 were the best ever. Our basketball and badminton teams
were overall champions in Division 1 of Hong Kong Island and the school
won the Jean Cassels' Trophy for the school with the best record in donating
blood during the year.
In addition to greater contact by overseas past students with their mother-
school, it is pleasing to report much activity and much cooperation with the
school on the part of the Past Students Association.
Wah Yan has much to be thankful to God for during its 60 years history，
but mention must be made, in particular, of the loyalty of its past, its teachers
and the many members of its staff that have served so long in the school.
Principal.

34.t: A Short History of Wah Yan
1919 Wah Yan College was born in December at No. 60 Hollywood Road.
1921 The school moved to new premises, in Robinson Road.“
Owing to the increase in applications for admission a hranch school was opened in
Portland Street,Kowloon.
1928 The Kowloon branch school moved to Nelson Street.
First time in the history of the college, the no. of boys on roll reaches the total of
800- the biggest no. in any school in the colony then.
1932 The College was transferred to the care of the Society of Jesus on"22nd December.
The late Fr. R. W. Gallagher, S.J. was the first Rector.
A branch for Senior students was opened on Sth September in Austin Road, while
Junior Classes continued in Nelson Street, under Mr. Lim Hoy Lan. Austin Road
had a short life as it closed on 9th December, the day after the Japanese invasion.
War- Wah Yan basement being turned into Red Cross Station. School closed.
Ihe Whole terrace beyond the college on Robinson Rd. burned to the ground.
1945 Wah Yan College re-opened on Sth September. Later in the year a Chinese stream
（Wah Yan Midalle School） was addled.
1946 In March the organisation of the Wah Yan Dramatic Society commenced.The first
production was “The Thrice Promised Bride"，performed in the French Convent
Theatre. The Society was formally established in 1947.
On 8th September the school at Nelson Street re-opened, with 560 pupils on the roll.
The Boys' Club was opened on 15th November, with 19 boys.（Mr. Joseph Cheung
helped at the beginning and is still with the Club.）
1918 The Night School was started on I7th February.
1949 An afternoon school opened, with more than 700 boys enrolled.
On I0th October the site for the new College in Waterloo Road was blessed.
1950 The Chinese Section of the school was closed down.
The Governor, Sir Alexander Grantham, opened Wah Yan College, Kowloon, on
12th December.
The Afternoon School in Wah Yan, Hong Kong, closed.
On 7th October the foundation stone of Wah Yan College, Queen's Road East, was
blessed and laid.
Formal opening of Wah Yan College, Queen's Road East, was performed on 27th
September by His Excellency the Gover nor, Sir Alexander Grantham.

96.t: We were all Shocked and saddened by the
sudden death of Fr. Martin Gryan on
Saturday I6th December 1978. Fr. Cryan had
finished a week of teaching in apparent good
health, and even on Saturday he did not seem
to be ill. Just shortly before he died he com-
plained of
feeling unwell
and
then, very
quickly he passed away peacefully.
Most of the readers of this obituary will
have known Fr. Cryan as a teacher, a devoted
helpful teacher.
The speed with which the
news of his death spread, and the reaction of
the students gave clear evidence of the respect
which they had tor him. On Sunday morning
there was a much larger attendance than usual
in the College Chapel; many boys returned to
the school to pray for their beloved teacher.
Among the congregation there was one past
student who had returned from England only
the night before.
Why was Fr. Cryan so respected by the
students！
I think the principal reason
was
that they realised he was fully devoted to their
welfare and intensely interested in them. As
a teacher, principally of biology, he knew his
subject thoroughly and was always on the look-
out for new ways of presenting his material to
make it more easily understood by his pupils；
he made a point of explaining everything as
Cearly as possible in Cass, and if there were
some who still did not understand, he was
ready to. spend time after class, helping them
with their difficulties.
It was quite common to
see Fr. Cryan
sitting at a table, with several textbooks and
encyclopedias open before him; he would be
checking and cross-checking some point of
information to make sure he had the latest and
most accurate information. This was typical
of him.
He had a very sharp, enquiring mind
and would go to great trouble to achieve the
greatest possible accuracy and then seek ways
of communicating that knowledge as clearly as
possible. Frequently, one saw him carrying
out experiments on plants to verify the
accuracy of some piece of information, and he
had no
hesitation in contradicting some
accepted biological statement.“That's what
the books say, but they're wrong. I tried it
out, and I know”， he would assert.
Along with accuracy of information, order
was a very important factor in Fr. Cryan's
make-up.
This desire for order seemed at
times to be excessive; not all agreed with his
insistence on such strict discipline, but it had
to be admitted that it all had a purpose. For
him learning was something serious and had to
be taken seriously.
In class he would not
tolerate any distraction. Yet, if a boy wanted
to sleep in class that was all right with Fr.
Cryan, provided the rest of the class wasn't dis-
turbed.
This explained a good deal of his
popularity - he was genunely trying to De
helpful. For this reason, too, ne was sougnt
Out for personal advice and direction which
were very much valued.
Fr. Cryan was a dedicated priest, and he
valued his priesthood highly. He gave to the
preparation of his sermons the same care and
attention to detail he gave to his teaching.
As
a result, he was recognised as an excellent
preacher. His sermons were prepared with
very great care, the material was solid and well
organised, and presented in a logical and
interesting fashion. It was prefectly clear that
what he said in sermons was the expression of
his own convictions; he would never be accused
of merely repeating another's ideas or express-
ing himself in cliches. He was interesting to
listen to and hadn't the slightest difhiculty
holding his audience.
Fr. Cryan's interests were many and varied.
Although a specialist in biology, he had a keen
interest in history and on occasion taught his-
tory even at Form Six level. Ihe countryside，
the open air, the night sky - all fascinated
him. After attending the Educators' Social
Action Workshop in Kyoto, Japan, he was a
very active member of the Educators' Social
Action Council in Hong Kong:In fact, at the
time_ of his death he was helping to compile
for E.S.A.C. a handbook on Counselling Ser-
vices in Hong, Kong.
As a Jesuit, Fr. Cryan was a very valuable
member of the Wah Yan community; he was
a good team-worker and he usually had an
interesting- and frequently a chalenging -
contribution to make to any discussion. One
indication of how much he is missed by the
Jesuits Is the number of times his names came
up in conversation - clear testimony of how
much he is missed by us all.
May God grant to Fr. Cryan the reward
of his Iabours.
